```{r}
library(tidyverse)

library(patchwork)
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)

data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)

noaa_missing_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_proportion"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    missing_percent = round(missing_proportion * 100, 2)
  )

noaa_missing_df

```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables. Each row represents a daily record from a weather station in New York State. The variables include station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and maximum and minimum temperatures. Missing data are an issue, especially for temperature: about 43.7% of values are missing for both maximum and minimum temperatures. Precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth have approximately 5.62%, 14.7%, and 22.8% missing values, respectively. Station ID and date have no missing values. The temperature variables are currently stored as character values and need to be converted to numeric.

### Data clean 

```{r}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

snow_frequency_df =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)

head(snow_frequency_df, 10)
```

I created separate variables for year, month, and day. I converted the temperature variables from character to numeric and changed their units to degrees Celsius. I also converted precipitation to millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth were already recorded in millimeters.

The most common snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. This is expected because many station-day records have no snowfall. The most common nonzero values are 25, 13, and 51 mm. These are close to 1, 0.5, and 2 inches, which suggests that unit conversion and rounding may contribute to their high frequencies.

### Make a two-panel plot 

```{r}
noaa_monthly_df =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(month = 
           factor(
             month,
             levels = c(1, 7),
             labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )
```

```{r}
noaa_monthly_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Daily Maximum Temperature by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Monthly mean daily maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) 
```

July is much warmer than January. Temperatures vary across stations, but many stations show similar changes from year to year. January also appears to have larger year-to-year changes than July. There are a few unusually low values, including a July value around 14°C in the late 1980s. These observations may reflect local conditions, limited daily records, or data quality issues and would need further checking. A clear long-term trend is not obvious from this plot.

### Make another two-panel plot 

```{r}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Daily minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Daily maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Daily snowfall (mm)"
  )

temperature_plot + snowfall_plot
```

I used a two-dimensional histogram because the dataset contains many observations. Points would overlap heavily in a scatterplot. The fill color shows the number of observations in each bin, making the concentration of records easier to see.

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship. Most observations form a diagonal band, but a few extreme values are far from the main pattern. Some records also appear to have minimum temperatures higher than maximum temperatures. These observations would need further checking.

For snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, the distributions are similar across most years. The median is around 25 mm in most years, although some years, such as 2006, have a narrower interquartile range. There is no clear long-term change in the distributions shown. This plot describes snowfall amounts on the selected days, rather than total annual snowfall.
